##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The eternal Agni, with seven hotṛs, shone at the Gārhapatya; shining on the earth's lap, the uttaravedi, he sounds and never sleeps, being born from the araṇi wood.

*[Small differences in the bhāṣya block, kept as supplied: the verb is explained as प्रारोचत (*prārocata*) and later as आरोचत (*ārocata*), whereas the Ṛk has अरोचत (*arocata*).]*

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- सनकात् (*sanakāt*)—the eternal Agni
- सप्तहोता (*saptahotā*)—having seven hotṛs
- प्रारोचत (*prārocata*)—shone
- यतः (*yataḥ*)—when
- मातुः (*mātuḥ*)—of the mother, the earth
- उपस्थे (*upasthe*)—which is the lap
- ऊधनि (*ūdhani*)—in the place of the uttaravedi
- अशोचत् (*aśocat*)—he shone, then
- सुरणः (*suraṇaḥ*)—he makes a sound
- यत् (*yat*)—for which reason
- असुरस्य (*asurasya*)—of the wood in the form of araṇi
- जठरात् (*jaṭharāt*)—from the belly
- अजायत (*ajāyata*)—he was born (therefore)
- दिवेदिवे (*divedive*)—every day; न निमिषति (*na nimiṣati*)—without sleeping, he is awake for the sacrifice. *[The word for "when" is printed यतः (*yataḥ*) here, whereas the Ṛk has यत् (*yat*); as supplied.]*

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The eternal Agni, having seven hotṛs, shone. When Agni shone in the place of the uttaravedi, which is the udder of his mother the earth, he then makes a sound. Because he was born from the belly of the wood in the form of araṇi, he is awake every day for the sacrifice, without sleeping.

*[In the supplied text the English-translation label of this Ṛk is printed as "English Ttranslation" and stands directly after the Bhāvārtha; as supplied.]*

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Agni, who has seven ministering priests, shines eternally : when he has blazed upon the bosom and lap of his mother (earth), he is vociferous (with delight) : day by day he never slumbers after he is born from the interior of the (spark) emitting wood.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

सनकात् सप्तहोता प्ररोचत (*sanakāt saptahotā prarocata*)—For the word सनकात् (*sanakāt*) the meaning "eternal, one who has existed for a very long time" is explained, and the meaning is described that the ancient Agni shone as the one with seven hotṛs, in the place called Gārhapatya in the sacrificial hall. *[The verb is printed here as प्ररोचत (*prarocata*); as supplied.]*

*[The supplied text of this window ends here, at the foot of page 620; the Special Topics of this Ṛk may continue in the next window.]*

### Printed p. 621

*(Ṛk 14, Special Topics, continued from the previous page; the same entry goes on:)* The word सप्तहोता (*saptahotā*) has been explained with सप्तहोतारो दोतृका यस्य (*saptahotāro dotṛkā yasya*) *[the word for "hotṛs" is printed with a different first letter from the bhāṣya; as supplied]* as meaning that Agni has as his sacrificers the seven ṛtvijs beginning with the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu. Yāska, citing the Ṛk दक्षस्य वादिते जन्मनि व्रते राजाना मित्रावरुणा विवाससि । अतूर्तपंथाः पुरुरथो अर्यमा सप्तहोता विषुरूपाषु जन्मसु ॥ (*dakṣasya vādite janmani vrate rājānā mitrāvaruṇā vivāsasi | atūrtapaṃthāḥ pururatho aryamā saptahotā viṣurūpāṣu janmasu ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-64-5), has commented: सप्तहोता सप्तास्मै रश्मयो रसानभि सन्नामयंति, सप्तनमृषयस्सुवंतीति वा । (*saptahotā saptāsmai raśmayo rasānabhi sannāmayaṃti, saptanamṛṣayassuvaṃtīti vā |*) Durgācārya: सप्तरश्मयः अस्मै रसानभिसन्नामयंति तदस्य सप्तहोतृत्वं (*saptaraśmayaḥ asmai rasānabhisannāmayaṃti tadasya saptahotṛtvaṃ*) — the seven rays give room for the waters to be drawn up, and so the state of having seven hotṛs comes about. Or वसिष्ठाद्याः सप्तऋषयः एनमाह्वयंति, नमंति, स्तुवंति तद्वा अस्य सप्तहोतृत्वं (*vasiṣṭhādyāḥ saptaṛṣayaḥ enamāhvayaṃti, namaṃti, stuvaṃti tadvā asya saptahotṛtvaṃ*) (Ni. 11-23): the seven ṛṣis beginning with Vasiṣṭha invoke this Agni, bow to him and praise him, and for that reason the seven-hotṛship of Agni is also fitting; so he has explained.

मातुरुपस्थे अशोचदूधनि (*māturupasthe aśocadūdhani*)—पृथिव्याः उत्संगे तत्रापि ऊधस्साने उत्तरवेद्यां अशोभत । (*pṛthivyāḥ utsaṃge tatrāpi ūdhassāne uttaravedyāṃ aśobhata |*) Yāska has read the word मातृ (*mātṛ*) among the names of rivers (Ni. 2-24). Having commented with माता अंतरिक्षं निर्मियंते अर्स्मिन् भूतानि (*mātā aṃtarikṣaṃ nirmiyaṃte arsmin bhūtāni*) (Ni. 2-8) *[the fourth word is printed ಅರ್ಸ್ಮಿನ್; as supplied]* he has explained its use in the sense of the sky (antarikṣa). And in the Ṛk अंजंति त्वामध्वरे देवयंतो वनस्पते मधुना दैव्येन । यदूर्ध्वस्तिष्ठा द्रविणेह धत्ताद्यद्वा क्षयो मातुरस्या उपस्थे ॥ (*aṃjaṃti tvāmadhvare devayaṃto vanaspate madhunā daivyena | yadūrdhvastiṣṭhā draviṇeha dhattādyadvā kṣayo māturasyā upasthe ‖*) *[the reference after this verse is printed broken: an unfinished "(Ṛ. Saṃ." and then, on the next line, "(Mi. Saṃ. 3-8-1)"; as supplied]* he has commented मातुः पृथिव्याः उपस्थे उपरि (*mātuḥ pṛthivyāḥ upasthe upari*). Just as for the word उपस्थे (*upasthe*) the meaning उपरि (*upari*) (above) is given, at अपामुपस्थे (*apāmupasthe*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-8-4) *[the quotation mark opened before this word is not closed in the supplied text]* he has also described the meaning: अपामुपस्थ उपस्थाने यत्रोपगम्य तिष्ठंत्यापः सोऽपामुपस्थः अंतरिक्षलोकः (*apāmupastha upasthāne yatropagamya tiṣṭhaṃtyāpaḥ so 'pāmupasthaḥ aṃtarikṣalokaḥ*) — the region of the sky where the waters gather together.

गोरूध उद्धततरं भवति उपोन्नद्धमिति वा स्नेहानुप्रदानसामान्याद्रात्रिरप्यूथ उच्यते (*gorūdha uddhatataraṃ bhavati uponnaddhamiti vā snehānupradānasāmānyādrātrirapyūtha ucyate*) (Ni. 6-19). The udder region of the cow is higher than the other limbs. The meaning of the word for "udder" has been explained by Yāska as being connected in some manner with the abdominal region of the cow. It is further said that, because the night pours down frost-water so as to favour the growth of herbs and trees, the night too is denoted by that word. Here Sāyaṇa has explained the meaning thus: Agni, produced by churning in the araṇis, when he shines in the uttaravedi of the sacrificial hall, which is the place of the udder in the lap of the earth, सुरणः (*suraṇaḥ*) makes a pleasing sound,

### Printed p. 622

*(Continued from the previous page; the sentence begun there goes on:)* and सर्वः कमनीयतया दृश्यमानः (*sarvaḥ kamanīyatayā dṛśyamānaḥ*) appears pleasing to everyone, and दिवे दिवे न निमिषति (*dive dive na nimiṣati*) every day, that is, always, he stays alert (awake) in the sacrificial hall, in the sacrifice, to receive the oblation; thus he has explained the meaning.

सुरणः (*suraṇaḥ*)—For this word Sāyaṇa has commented with सुष्टु रणयति शब्दयतीति सुरणः (*suṣṭu raṇayati śabdayatīti suraṇaḥ*). Yāska, at रथं नु मारुतं वयं श्रवस्युमा हुवामहे । आ यस्मिन् तस्थौ सुरणानि बिभ्रती सचा मरुत्सु रोदसी ॥ (*rathaṃ nu mārutaṃ vayaṃ śravasyumā huvāmahe | ā yasmin tasthau suraṇāni bibhratī sacā marutsu rodasī ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-56-8), has described the meaning सुरणानि सुष्टु रमणीयानि उदकानि (*suraṇāni suṣṭu ramaṇīyāni udakāni*) (pleasing waters).

असुरस्य जठरादजायत (*asurasya jaṭharādajāyata*)—Yāska has read the word असुर (*asura*) among the names of the cloud (Ni. 2-22). From this the meaning "cloud" can also result. Having quoted असुराः असुरताः स्थानेष्वस्ताः, स्थानेभ्य इतिवा, अपिवा असुरिति प्राणनामास्तः शरीरे भवति तेन तद्वंतः । सोर्दॆवानसृजत तत् सुराणां सुरत्वं आसोरसुरानसृजत तदसुराणामसुरत्वमिति विज्ञायते (*asurāḥ asuratāḥ sthāneṣvastāḥ, sthānebhya itivā, apivā asuriti prāṇanāmāstaḥ śarīre bhavati tena tadvaṃtaḥ | sordèvānasṛjata tat surāṇāṃ suratvaṃ āsorasurānasṛjata tadasurāṇāmasuratvamiti vijñāyate*) *[no reference is printed; the word beginning the second sentence of the quotation has a short vowel sign after its second letter; as supplied]* he has explained the meaning of the word asura, saying that it can also mean "asuras" (demons). Sāyaṇa, with अग्नेःप्रेरकस्य अरणीरूपस्य काष्ठस्य (*agneḥprerakasya araṇīrūpasya kāṣṭhasya*) (the particular wood that is the cause of the manifestation of Agni exists in the form of the araṇi), has described the meaning of the word asura, and has described that, because Agni is born from the middle region of this araṇi for the performance of the sacrificial rites, he is always awake.

##### Grammar (Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā)

अरोचत (*arocata*)—रुच दीप्तौ (*ruca dīptau*), a dhātu. A form ending in लज् (*laj*) , third person singular. Since it stands after an अतिजंत (*atijaṃta*) , the nighāta accent comes.

अशोचत् (*aśocat*)—शुच दीप्तौ (*śuca dīptau*), a dhātu. A form ending in लज् (*laj*), third person singular. Since there is the connection with yat (यद्योग (*yadyoga*)), the nighāta accent does not come. Since the augment aṭ (अडागम (*aḍāgama*)) is udātta, the word becomes ādyudātta.

ऊधनि (*ūdhani*)—ऊधस् (*ūdhas*) is the word; a form ending in the locative singular. In the Vedic language the substitution of nakāra for sakāra has come.

मिषति (*miṣati*)—मिषु सेचने (*miṣu secane*), a dhātu. Laṭ, a form ending in the third person singular. The nighāta accent for a verb ending (तिजंत (*tijaṃta*)) comes.

सुरणः (*suraṇaḥ*)—रण शब्दे (*raṇa śabde*), a dhātu. By तत्करोति तदाचष्टॆ (*tatkaroti tadācaṣṭè*) *[the last letter is printed with the short vowel sign; as supplied]* the suffix ṇic on it. After the ṇic-ending form, by ईषद्दुःसुषु (*īṣadduḥsuṣu*) (Pā. Sū. 3-3-126) *[the abbreviation is printed with a comma after Pā; as supplied]* the suffix khal, when su is the upapada.

### Printed p. 623

*(Grammar of Ṛk 14, continued from the previous page.)* By शेरनिटि (*śeraniṭi*) (Pā. Sū. 6-4-51) loss of ṇic. Since the suffix is lit, by लिति (*liti*) (Pā. Sū. 6-1-193) the udātta accent comes to what stands before the suffix.

दिवेदिवे (*divedive*)—By नित्यवीप्सयोः (*nityavīpsayoḥ*) (Pā. Sū. 8-1-4), when the doubling (द्विर्पचन (*dvirpacana*)) comes, by अनुदात्तंच (*anudāttaṃca*) (Pā. Sū. 8-1-3) the latter part becomes entirely anudātta.

आसुरस्य (*āsurasya*) *[printed with a long first vowel; as supplied]*—असु क्षेपणे (*asu kṣepaṇe*), a dhātu. By असेरुरन् (*aseruran*) (U. Sū. 1-42) the suffix uran. अस्यति इति असुरः (*asyati iti asuraḥ*). Since the suffix is nit, by इत्न्यत्यादिर्नित्यं (*itnyatyādirnityaṃ*) (Pā. Sū. 6-1-178) the ādyudātta accent comes. A form ending in the genitive singular.

जठरात् (*jaṭharāt*)—जनी प्रादुर्भावे (*janī prādurbhāve*), a dhātu. By जनेररष्य च (*janeraraṣya ca*) (U. Sū. 5-716) the suffix ara *[the sūtra and its number differ from those given in the bhāṣya block of the previous page; as supplied]*. The substitution of ठकार (*ṭhakāra*) for the end of the dhātu *[the bhāṣya block names another letter here; as supplied]*. The form जठर (*jaṭhara*) results. The ādyudātta accent of the suffix comes.

अजायत (*ajāyata*)—जनी प्रादुर्भावे (*janī prādurbhāve*), a dhātu, of the divādi class. A form ending in लज् (*laj*), third person singular. By ज्ञाजनोर्जा (*jñājanorjā*) (Pā. Sū. 7-3-79) the substitution जा (*jā*) for the dhātu. The vikaraṇa श्यन् (*śyan*). Since there is the connection with yat (यद्योग (*yadyoga*)), the nighāta accent does not come. Since the augment aṭ (अडागम (*aḍāgama*)) is udātta, the word becomes ādyudātta.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The Kuśikas, who fight the rite-obstructing asuras, know the world, recite hymns and kindle Agni, each in his own house, with oblations.

*[In this bhāṣya block the gloss ends with a double danda sign attached to its last word, and the grammatical notes on the words follow in the same block; as supplied.]*

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- मरुतां इव (*marutāṃ iva*)—like a host of Maruts striking down the enemies
- प्रयाः (*prayāḥ*)—driving the enemies away
- अमित्रायुधः (*amitrāyudhaḥ*)—those who fight with the asuras who obstruct rites
- ब्रह्मणः (*brahmaṇaḥ*)—to Brahmā, the world-creator *[the Kannada compound is printed as "world-created"; rendered as the sense requires, as supplied]*
- प्रथमजाः (*prathamajāḥ*)—those born first
- कुशिकासः (*kuśikāsaḥ*)—the ṛṣis born in the Kuśika gotra
- विश्वं (*viśvaṃ*)—the whole world, of the nature of the unmoving and the moving; विदुः इत् (*viduḥ it*)—they indeed know
- द्युम्नवत् (*dyumnavat*)—accompanied by an oblation
- ब्रह्म (*brahma*)—the hymn
- एरिरे (*erire*)—they recite around Agni (and)
- दमे (*dame*)—in their several houses
- एकएकः (*ekaekaḥ*)—every single ṛṣi
- अग्निं (*agniṃ*)—Agni
- समाधिरे (*samādhire*)—they make him blaze fully

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Like a host of Maruts striking down the enemies, driving the enemies away, fighting with the asuras who obstruct rites, and born first to Brahmā, the world-creator, the ṛṣis born in the Kuśika gotra know the whole world, of the nature of the unmoving and the moving. (They) recite around Agni a hymn accompanied by an oblation. And in their several houses every single ṛṣi makes Agni blaze fully.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
The Kushikas, the first-born of Brahma, armed against enemies like the energies of the Maruts, comprehend the universe : they have uttered the prayer accompanied by the oblation : they have one by one lighted Agni in this dwelling.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In this Ṛk the greatness of the ṛṣis born in the Kuśika gotra is stated, and the matter of their worshipping Agni (serving him with worship) is also stated.

### Printed p. 625

*(No label stands at the head of this page; the text is taken as the continuation of the Special Topics of Ṛk 15.)*

मरुतामिव प्रयाः अमित्रायुधः (*marutāmiva prayāḥ amitrāyudhaḥ*)—मरुतां देवानां प्रकर्षेण शत्रुवनभियांतीति प्रयाः बलानि शत्रुवाणं हंत्यणि तद्वत् कर्मविघ्नकारिणां पापानां हंतारः (*marutāṃ devānāṃ prakarṣeṇa śatruvanabhiyāṃtīti prayāḥ balāni śatruvāṇaṃ haṃtyaṇi tadvat karmavighnakāriṇāṃ pāpānāṃ haṃtāraḥ*) Just as the armies of the gods destroy enemies exceedingly, they destroy also the sins that cause obstruction in the performance of good rites; in the same way those born in the Kuśika gotra कर्मविघ्नकारिभिरसुरैः सह योद्धारः, यव्वा अमित्राणि पापानि तैस्सह योद्धारः । (*karmavighnakāribhirasuraiḥ saha yoddhāraḥ, yavvā amitrāṇi pāpāni taissaha yoddhāraḥ |*) *[the word for "or" is printed with a different spelling from the bhāṣya; as supplied]* having fought with the asuras who cause obstruction to rites, or with sins, will destroy them; thus it is described, and they are explained as full of greatness like the armies of the gods.

ब्रह्मणः प्रथमजाः कुशिकासः विश्वं विदुरित् (*brahmaṇaḥ prathamajāḥ kuśikāsaḥ viśvaṃ vidurit*)—सर्वस्य जगतः स्रष्टुः प्रथममुत्पन्नाः कुशिकगोत्रोत्पन्ना ऋषयः विश्वं स्थावरजंगमात्मकं सर्वं जगत् जानंत्येव (*sarvasya jagataḥ sraṣṭuḥ prathamamutpannāḥ kuśikagotrotpannā ṛṣayaḥ viśvaṃ sthāvarajaṃgamātmakaṃ sarvaṃ jagat jānaṃtyeva*) The ṛṣis born in the Kuśika gotra, born first from Brahmā who has created the whole universe, know all that exists in the form of the unmoving and the moving, the whole nature of the world; thus their greatness is indicated through the description of their origin.

द्युम्नवत् ब्रह्म एरिरे (*dyumnavat brahma erire*)—The word द्युम्न (*dyumna*) and the word ब्रह्म (*brahma*) are stated among the names of wealth (Ni. 3-9). It has been explained: द्युम्नं द्योततेर्यशो वा अन्नं ना (*dyumnaṃ dyotateryaśo vā annaṃ nā*) *[the last word is printed so; as supplied]*. तेऽमी कुशिकाः हविर्युक्तं ब्रह्म स्तोत्रं अग्नये आ समंतात् प्रेरयंति (*te 'mī kuśikāḥ haviryuktaṃ brahma stotraṃ agnaye ā samaṃtāt prerayaṃti*) These ṛṣis born in the Kuśika gotra praise Agni with hymns and offer oblations to Agni; thus the meaning is explained.

दमे एकएकः अग्निं समाधिरे (*dame ekaekaḥ agniṃ samādhire*)—स्वे स्वे गृहे एकैकः भूत्वा अग्निं आज्याद्याहुतिभिः सम्यक् दीपयंति (*sve sve gṛhe ekaikaḥ bhūtvā agniṃ ājyādyāhutibhiḥ samyak dīpayaṃti*) These ṛṣis, each one separately in his own house, worship Agni with oblations beginning with ghee and satisfy him; thus it is described.

##### Grammar (Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā)

अमित्रायुधः (*amitrāyudhaḥ*)—युध संप्रहारे (*yudha saṃprahāre*), a dhātu. The suffix क्विप् (*kvip*). अमित्रैः युध्यंति इति अमित्रायुधः (*amitraiḥ yudhyaṃti iti amitrāyudhaḥ*). By अन्येषामपिदृश्यते (*anyeṣāmapidṛśyate*) (Pā. Sū. 6-3-137) lengthening of the former member. By गतिकारकोपपदात्‌कृत् (*gatikārakopapadātkṛt*) (Pā. Sū. 9-2-139) *[the number is printed so; as supplied]* the accent natural to the later member that ends in a kṛt suffix comes.

प्रयाः (*prayāḥ*)—या प्रापणे (*yā prāpaṇe*), a dhātu. By अन्येभ्योपिदृश्यंते (*anyebhyopidṛśyaṃte*) (Pā. Sū. 3-2-75) the suffix विच् (*vic*). Since the former member is a gati, the accent natural to the later member that ends in a kṛt suffix comes.

प्रथमजाः (*prathamajāḥ*)—जनी प्रादुर्भावे (*janī prādurbhāve*), a dhātu. By जनसनख (*janasanakha*) (Pā. Sū. 6-4-42) *[the sūtra is printed in this cut-off form, with a dash before the reference; as supplied]* the suffix विट् (*viṭ*). When it follows, by विड्वनोरनुनासिकस्यात् (*viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*) (Pā. Sū. 6-4-41) the dhātu takes आत्व (*ātva*). The accent natural to the later member that ends in a kṛt suffix comes.

विदु: (*vidu:*)—विद ज्ञाने (*vida jñāne*), a dhātu, लट् (*laṭ*). By विदोलट्योवा (*vidolaṭyovā*) (Pā. Sū. 3-4-83) *[the sūtra is printed in a form different from the bhāṣya block; as supplied]* for झि (*jhi*) the substitution उसादेश (*usādeśa*). Since it stands after an अतिजंत (*atijaṃta*) , the nighāta accent comes.

### Printed p. 626

*(Grammar of Ṛk 15, continued from the previous page. A stray line consisting of the number 79 stands at the foot of the previous page; kept as supplied.)*

ईरिरे (*īrire*)—ईत गत् (*īta gat*) , a dhātu, लिट् (*liṭ*). Although it begins with ij, since this is prohibited in आमंत्रे (*āmaṃtre*) (Pā. Sū. 3-1-35), ām does not come. A form ending in the third person plural. The nighāta accent of the verb ending comes.

दमे (*dame*)—दमु उपशमे (*damu upaśame*), a dhātu. When the sense of instrument appears, the suffix घञ् (*ghañ*). By नोदात्तोपदेशस्य (*nodāttopadeśasya*) (Pā. Sū. 7-3-34) the prohibition of vṛddhi comes. On that ground, by इत्त्यादिनिर्त्यं (*ittyādinirtyaṃ*) the ādyudātta accent comes.

ईधिरे (*īdhire*)—इइंधी दीप्तौ (*iiṃdhī dīptau*) *[printed with a doubled first vowel; as supplied]*, a dhātu, लिट् (*liṭ*). For the third person plural the substitution इरेच् (*irec*). Because the dhātu has a conjunct consonant and the लिटि (*liṭi*) has no क्वित्व (*kvitva*), by इंदिभवतिभ्यांच (*iṃdibhavatibhyāṃca*) the किद्वद्भाव (*kidvadbhāva*) comes *[the reference after the sūtra is printed with a double danda in place of its middle number; as supplied, not quoted here]*, and by अनिदितांहलउ (*aniditāṃhalau*) loss of the nakāra that stands as upadhā. Since it stands after an अतिजंत (*atijaṃta*), the nighāta accent comes.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- होतः (*hotaḥ*)—performer of the oblation
- चिकित्सः (*cikitsaḥ*)—one who has knowledge about rites: O Agni
- अद्य (*adya*)—at this time of the rite

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Agni, performer of the oblation and one who has knowledge about rites: in the sacrifice of the form of Jyotiṣṭoma and the like, which is being performed at this time of the rite, seeking what help do we choose you and approach you? Therefore convey our oblations to the gods in this rite so that they are firm. And you, of tranquil mind, satisfy the gods too with the oblations. Knowing the purpose of this sacrifice, you, the wise one, aiming at the Soma offered by us, be pleased to come.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Agni, offerer of oblations, cognizant of rites, inasmuch as we have recourse to you to-day in this progressing sacrifice, therefore steadily convey (the offering to the gods), or tranquilly be at rest, and knowing (the purport of our acts), and wise (in all respects), approach (and accept) the Soma libation.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

होतः (*hotaḥ*)—Because Agni performs the oblation he is described as the accomplisher of the oblation, and चिकित्सः (*cikitsaḥ*) as one who has knowledge of the sacrifice; he is addressed with these words.

अद्य प्रयति अस्मिन् यज्ञे त्वा अवृणीमहि (*adya prayati asmin yajñe tvā avṛṇīmahi*)—Agni, who is the accomplisher of the oblation and has knowledge of the sacrifice, is invited by the sacrificers in the sacrifice now going on, in order that the sacrifice may be performed *[the Kannada word for "performed" is broken across the page boundary; the sentence continues on the next page]*

##### Grammar (Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā)

प्रयति (*prayati*)—इण् गतौ (*iṇ gatau*), a dhātu. The substitute *śatṛ* for *laṭ*. A form ending in the singular of the seventh case. Since the case ending comes after the *śatṛ* that has no *nuṃ*, by शतुरनुमोनद्यजादी (*śaturanumonadyajādī*) (Pā. Sū. 6-1-173) the udātta accent comes to it.

चिकित्त्वः (*cikittvaḥ*) *[printed with a doubled t; as supplied]*—कित ज्ञाने (*kita jñāne*), a dhātu; for *liṭ* the substitution क्वसुरादेश (*kvasurādeśa*); for the dhātu द्वित्वादि (*dvitvādi*); in the vocative रुत्व (*rutva*) and visarga. By आमंत्रितस्यच (*āmaṃtritasyaca*) the nighāta accent comes *[the last Kannada word of the entry is printed with a slip; the sense is as given]*.

अवृणीमहि (*avṛṇīmahi*)—वृञ् वरणे (*vṛñ varaṇe*), a dhātu. In the क्र्यादि (*kryādi*) class, in लज् (*laj*) , first person plural, the suffix महिज् (*mahij*) . By क्र्यादिभ्यः श्ना (*kryādibhyaḥ śnā*) (Pā. Sū. 3-1-81) the vikaraṇa श्ना (*śnā*). Because the suffix has the extension of the status of जतित्वातिदेश (*jatitvātideśa*) , by ईहल्यघोः (*īhalyaghoḥ*) (Pā. Sū. 6-4-113) the ईत्व (*ītva*) for the ā of the vikaraṇa. Because an address stands before it, by आमंत्रितंपूर्वमविद्यमानवत् (*āmaṃtritaṃpūrvamavidyamānavat*) it is as if not there although it is there, so it comes to stand as if at the beginning of the pāda, and the nighāta accent does not come. The augment अडागम (*aḍāgama*) being udātta, the word becomes ādyudātta.

अयाः (*ayāḥ*)—या प्रापणे (*yā prāpaṇe*), a dhātu. In लज् (*laj*) second person singular the suffix सिप् (*sip*). By इतश्च (*itaśca*) (Pā. Sū. 3-4-100) the final i is elided, and the stem takes the augment अडागम (*aḍāgama*). Since it stands after an अतिजंत (*atijaṃta*), the nighāta accent comes.

अशमिष्ठाः (*aśamiṣṭhāḥ*)—शमु उपशमने (*śamu upaśamane*), a dhātu. By हेतुमतिच (*hetumatica*) (Pā. Sū. 3-1-26) *ṇic*. After the *ṇic* ending, in लुज् (*luj*) second person singular the suffix थास् (*thās*). Because the option is laid down by स्यसिच्‌सीयुट् (*syasicsīyuṭ*) (Pā. Sū. 6-4-62), the augment इडागम (*iḍāgama*) comes to *sic*. By असिद्धवदत्राभात् (*asiddhavadatrābhāt*) (Pā. Sū. 6-4-22) this is as if not accomplished, and so by शेरनिटि (*śeraniṭi*) (Pā. Sū. 6-4-51) elision comes to *ṇic*.

प्रजानन् (*prajānan*)—ज्ञा अवबोधने (*jñā avabodhane*), a dhātu. The substitute *śatṛ* for *laṭ*. Because it is read in the क्र्यादिगणपठित (*kryādigaṇapaṭhita*) group, the vikaraṇa श्ना (*śnā*). By श्नाभ्यस्तयोरातः (*śnābhyastayorātaḥ*) (Pā. Sū. 6-4-112) elision of the ā of the vikaraṇa. By ज्ञाजनोर्जा (*jñājanorjā*) *[the sūtra is printed with a dash before its reference, and the reference with no stop after Pā; as supplied]* (Pā. Sū. 7-4-79) the substitution जादेश (*jādeśa*) for the dhātu. When the ādyudātta accent of the suffix has come, in the vicinity the accent natural to the later member that ends in a kṛt suffix comes.

### Printed p. 629

*(Grammar of Ṛk 16, continued from the previous page.)*

याहि (*yāhi*)—या प्रापणे (*yā prāpaṇe*), a dhātu. A form ending in the second person singular of *loṭ*. The nighāta accent of a verb form comes.

विद्वान् (*vidvān*)—विद ज्ञाने (*vida jñāne*), a dhātu. The substitute *śatṛ* for *laṭ*. By विदेः शतुर्वसुः (*videḥ śaturvasuḥ*) (Pā. Sū. 7-1-36) the substitution वसुरादेश (*vasurādeśa*) for it. The word विद्वस् (*vidvas*) results. When सु (*su*) follows, the augment नुमागम (*numāgama*) because it is ugit. By the suffix accent the ā becomes udātta.

**Pīṭhike (Introduction)**

In this adhyāya, with the exception of the 33rd sūkta alone, all the remaining sūktas are addressed to Indra. Therefore the description concerning Indra, his deeds of valour, his companionship with the other gods and similar matters will be explained at length in this Pīṭhike.

*The origin of Indra; his mother and father, and his wife.*

Although the greatness of Indra is described in a most excellent and poetic style, nowhere is Indra described as a supreme god without birth. As has been observed on many earlier occasions, a mother and a father of Indra are specified. And the nature of the origin of Indra too

*[The supplied text of this window ends here, in the middle of a sentence; the Pīṭhike continues in the next window.]*

…has been praised at great length in many places. For example, in some of the mantras quoted below the matter of Indra's birth is stated.

"O Indra, on the very day you were born you drank the juice of the Soma plant that grows in the mountain region, and showed in it your great fondness. Your mother, who bore you and was young, gave you that Soma juice in the house of your father of great power, and satisfied you. This same Indra, as soon as he was born, when he approached his mother, found Soma juice in her breast-milk." (3-48-2, 3).

"O Indra, as the atmosphere is seen, your father is of very firm body. The begetter of Indra, who roars in the atmosphere and is steady like the earth, is a most skilful doer of deeds. Indra has the greatest devotion both toward his father and toward his mother." (8-17-4).

Although in the Purāṇas and elsewhere Indra is famous as one of the Ādityas and as the companion of Varuṇa, yet (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-85-4) in the other parts of the Ṛk-saṃhitā he is, for the most part, not described in this way, that is, as one of the Ādityas. In 4-26-1 his identity with Manu and Sūra is shown. In the mantras 8-82-1 and 4; 10-89-2 he is denoted by the word Sūra. In 2-30-1 he is described by the epithet Savitṛ.

In the Atharvaveda the description of Indra's power is given in the following words.

एकाष्टका तपसा तप्यमाना जजान गर्भं महिमानमिंद्रं । तेन देवा अषहंत शत्रून् हंता दस्यूनामभवच्छचीपतिः ॥ (*ekāṣṭakā tapasā tapyamānā jajāna garbhaṃ mahimānamiṃdraṃ | tena devā aṣahaṃta śatrūn haṃtā dasyūnāmabhavacchacīpatiḥ ‖*)

Having practised austerity of great power, Ekāṣṭakā bore Indra, who has greatness. By the help of this Indra the gods conquered their enemies. Indra, the lord of Śacī, became the slayer of the Dasyus.

*[A stray number, 80, stands at the end of this page in the supplied text; kept as supplied.]*

### Printed p. 634

In the Ṛk next to this one Ekāṣṭakā is declared to be the mother of Indra and Soma both, and the daughter of Prajāpati. In the Atharvaveda Indra's mother is addressed (6-38), but her name is not given. The Mahābhārata states that Indra is one of the sons born to Kaśyapa by Dākṣāyaṇī, the daughter of Dakṣa, who has the other name Aditi. (Ā. Pa.) In the Atharvaveda 8-58-4 he is called the son of truth (सूनुं सत्यस्य (*sūnuṃ satyasya*)).

In another place it is stated that Indra was created by the gods for the destruction of enemies. (3-49-1) (घनं वृत्राणां जनयंत देवाः (*ghanaṃ vṛtrāṇāṃ janayaṃta devāḥ*)).

(2-13-5; 3-51-8)

In the Puruṣasūkta it is stated that Indra was born, together with Agni, from the mouth of the Puruṣa. (मुखादिंद्रश्चाग्निश्च (*mukhādiṃdraścāgniśca*)).

(10-90-13)

In another place in the Ṛk-saṃhitā it is stated explicitly that Indra is one of the gods born of Soma.

(9-96-5)

Indra, of such valour, conquered heaven by the power of his austerity.

(10-167-1)

In the Brāhmaṇas such as the Śatapatha the story of the origin of Indra is set out in various ways. For example, the account in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa is as follows.

ता ना एताः प्रजापतेरधि देवताः असृज्यंत अग्निरिंद्रः सोमः परमेष्ठी प्राजापत्यः । ताः सहस्रायुषो जज्ञिरे । ता यथा नद्यै पारं परापश्येदेवं स्वस्यायुषः पारं वराचख्युः । (*tā nā etāḥ prajāpateradhi devatāḥ asṛjyaṃta agniriṃdraḥ somaḥ parameṣṭhī prājāpatyaḥ | tāḥ sahasrāyuṣo jajñire | tā yathā nadyai pāraṃ parāpaśyedevaṃ svasyāyuṣaḥ pāraṃ varācakhyuḥ |*)

(Śa. Bā. 11-1-6-14)

Agni, Indra, Soma and Pārameṣṭhi Prājāpatya: all of these are gods created by Prajāpati. All of them were born with a life of a thousand years. As a man can see the far bank of a river, in the same way all of them had the power to see beyond the end of their own life, it says. The account in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa states the matter of Indra's origin in this way.

प्रजापतिर्देवासुरानसृजत । स इंद्रमपि ना सृजत । तं देवा अब्रुवन् । इंद्रं नो जनयेति। सोऽब्रवीत्। यथाहं युष्माग् स्तपसासृक्षि। एवमिंद्रं जनयध्वमिति । ते तपोऽतप्यंत । त आत्मन्निंद्रमपश्यन् । तमब्रुवन् जायस्वीति । सोऽब्रवीत् । किंभागधेयमभि जनिष्य इति । (*prajāpatirdevāsurānasṛjata | sa iṃdramapi nā sṛjata | taṃ devā abruvan | iṃdraṃ no janayeti| so 'bravīt| yathāhaṃ yuṣmāg stapasāsṛkṣi| evamiṃdraṃ janayadhvamiti | te tapo 'tapyaṃta | ta ātmanniṃdramapaśyan | tamabruvan jāyasvīti | so 'bravīt | kiṃbhāgadheyamabhi janiṣya iti |*)

तून्त्संवत्सरं । प्रजाः पशून् । इमान्नोकानित्यब्रुवन् । तं वै माहुत्याप्रजनयतेत्यब्रवीत् । तं चतुर्होत्रा प्राजनयन् । (*tūntsaṃvatsaraṃ | prajāḥ paśūn | imānnokānityabruvan | taṃ vai māhutyāprajanayatetyabravīt | taṃ caturhotrā prājanayan |*)

(Tai. Brā. 2-2-3-3, 4).

Prajāpati created the gods and the Asuras, but did not create Indra. Then they prayed to Prajāpati, "Create Indra for us." Then he said to the gods, "In the way in which I, by the power of my austerity, caused all of you to come into being, in that same way you also, as the fruit of the toil of austerity, create Indra." Then all those gods practised austerity. Then they found Indra within themselves. Afterwards they told him to receive a share of the oblation. Then Indra said, "For what purpose must I manifest myself outside?" Then they said, "You should come into being for the nourishment of the seasons and the year, and for the protection of all of these: all beings and all worlds." But in another place in this same Brāhmaṇa there is a somewhat different account of the origin of Indra. That account is as follows.

प्रजापतिरिंद्रमसृजतानुजावरं देवानां । तं प्राहिणोत् । परेहि । एतेषां देवानामधिपतिरेधीति । तं देवा अब्रुवन् । कस्त्वमसि । वयं वै त्वच्छेयाग्ंसस्य इति । सोऽब्रवीत् । कस्त्वमसि वयं वै त्वच्छेयाग्ंसस्य इति मा देवा अवोचन्निति । अथ वा इदं तर्हि प्रजापतौ हर आसीत् । यदस्मिन्नादित्ये । तदेनमब्रवीत् । एतन्मे प्रयच्छ । अथाहमेतेषां देवानामधिपतिर्भविष्यामीति............ततो ना इंद्रोदेवानामधिपतिरभवत् ॥ (*prajāpatiriṃdramasṛjatānujāvaraṃ devānāṃ | taṃ prāhiṇot | parehi | eteṣāṃ devānāmadhipatiredhīti | taṃ devā abruvan | kastvamasi | vayaṃ vai tvaccheyāgṃsasya iti | so 'bravīt | kastvamasi vayaṃ vai tvaccheyāgṃsasya iti mā devā avocanniti | atha vā idaṃ tarhi prajāpatau hara āsīt | yadasminnāditye | tadenamabravīt | etanme prayaccha | athāhameteṣāṃ devānāmadhipatirbhaviṣyāmīti............tato nā iṃdrodevānāmadhipatirabhavat ‖*)

(Tai. Brā. 2-2-10-1-2).

*[In the Sanskrit above, a row of dots stands in the middle of the quotation in the supplied text; kept as supplied.]*

After creating all the gods, Prajāpati created Indra last and made him lord over all the remaining gods. Then the gods addressed Indra: "Who are you? When all of us are superior to you, how can you be lord over all of us?" Then Indra, explaining this situation, begged Prajāpati to provide him with the power of Prajāpati, which gives the qualification to be lord over all the gods. Afterwards he obtained their lordship, it is said. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā:

इंद्रो वै देवानामानुजावर आसीत्स प्रजापतिमुपाधावत्तस्मा एतग्ं षोडशिनं प्रायच्छत्तमगृह्णीत ततो वै सोग्रं देवतानां पर्यैत् (*iṃdro vai devānāmānujāvara āsītsa prajāpatimupādhāvattasmā etagṃ ṣoḍaśinaṃ prāyacchattamagṛhṇīta tato vai sograṃ devatānāṃ paryait*)

(Tai. Saṃ. 6-6-11-2).

Indra was the youngest of all the gods. Then he went to Prajāpati and, with the intention of obtaining his help and attaining lordship over the gods, he offered the Ṣoḍaśin. Then Prajāpati showed him favour. As a result Indra obtained an excellent qualification and became lord to the gods,

**Epithets showing Indra's physical and mental qualities.**

The epithets that describe Indra's extraordinary qualities are very abundant. First, the description of his youth and strength. This Indra is exceedingly young, and likewise ancient. He is exceedingly powerful and active.

(1-130-7; 2-22-4; 6-29-3; 8-24-9, 12; 8-57-7; 8-81-3).

There are also very many passages that describe Indra's warrior qualities: that he possesses kṣatriya valour, is radiant, ageless, victorious over everything, endowed with unlimited discernment, possesses unobstructed valour and vigour (ojas), and bears the thunderbolt.

(1-4-5 ; 1-16-9 ; 1-30-6 ; 15 ; 1-6-11 ; 1-81-2, 7 ; 1-84-2, 1-100-12; 1-102-6 ; 1-165-6 ; 2-21-1 to 3 ; 3-30-3 ; 3-32-7 ; 3-45-2! 3-46-1; 6-18-4 ; 7-20-4; 7-22-5 ; 8-81-5 ; 8-84-7 ; 19-103-3,1).

*[In the last reference the first number is printed as 19, and in the next-but-one reference below as 18 and in another as 201; all kept as supplied. The reference before the last has an exclamation mark where a semicolon would stand; as supplied.]*

In Indra's body there is ವೀತ್ಯ [the word is printed so; as supplied], in his arms strength, in his hand the thunderbolt, and in his head discernment.

(2-6-2).

Indra can assume many kinds of forms. All those forms are extremely beautiful, and they have the golden form of the sun.

(18-112-3).

### Printed p. 639

The seers who saw the Ṛk-saṃhitā, in describing this special beauty of Indra, have set out various similes. Among these the words सुशिप्र (*suśipra*) and शिप्रन् (*śipran*) are the chief. These words mean one who has excellent cheeks or nose. This is a personal quality of Indra.

(1-9-3, 1-29-2; 1-81-4, 1-101-10; 3-32-3 ; 3-36-10, 8-32-4, 24 ;
8-33-7 ; 8-55-4, 10-105-5 ; 3-30-3 ; 8-17-4 ; 8-81-4).

In 8-65-10 it is described that Indra, having obtained strength from the drinking of Soma, relishes the sweetness of the Soma-drinking by smacking his lips. Epithets such as हरिशिप्र (*hariśipra*), हरिकेश (*harikeśa*) and हरिश्मश्रु (*hariśmaśru*) are also exceedingly numerous. That is, they mean one who has golden cheeks, one who has golden hair, one who has golden facial hair.

(10-96_4, 9, 12; 10-96_5, 8 ; 10-23_4).

*[In these three references the hyphen before the last number is printed as an underscore; as supplied. When he is greatly delighted, the hairs of his face and beard bristle and move.

(201-17 ; 10-23-1).

(In 6-46-3 Indra is also described as thousand-faced.)

The whole form of this Indra is golden. In many places his form is described as हरिवर्पस् (*harivarpas*) and as हिरण्यय (*hiraṇyaya*) in form.

(10-96-1 ; 8-55-3 ; 1-7-2).

But in some other places it is also stated that he has आयसरूप (*āyasarūpa*), that is, a body made of steel.

(1-56-3 ; 10-96-4, 8).

His arms are spread out to a great distance. (पृथू करस्ना बहुला गभस्ती (*pṛthū karasnā bahulā gabhastī*))-

(6-19-3 ; 8-2 2-10 ; 8-70-1).

इंद्रस्य बाहू स्थविरौ युवानावनाधृष्ट्य सुप्रथितावसह्यौ । तौ युंजीत प्रथमौ योगे आगते याभ्यां जितमसुराणां सहो महत् ॥ (*iṃdrasya bāhū sthavirau yuvānāvanādhṛṣṭya suprathitāvasahyau | tau yuṃjīta prathamau yoge āgate yābhyāṃ jitamasurāṇāṃ saho mahat ‖*)

**Indra's chariot and horses.**

Indra, seated in his golden chariot, holding in his hand a golden whip, sets out on his journey. That chariot has a thousand supporting pillars.

(6-29-2; 8-1-24; 8-58-16).

This chariot of Indra has a speed greater than that of the mind.

(10-112-2).

*[The reference is printed in Telugu numerals; rewritten letter for letter in Kannada numerals in kn.md.]*

This chariot is drawn by a pair of horses that are golden in colour, of unobstructed strength, and neighing wonderfully. They have manes of golden form. They are as attractive as peacock feathers. These horses travel with great speed and can travel to a great distance. Just as a ಗಿಡಗ (the supplied word; as supplied) can travel with the help of its wings, in the same way this Indra too can fly about all over the intermediate space with the help of his horses.

(1-30-16 ; 1-81-3 ; 1-10-3 ; 1-82-6 ; 8-17-2 ; 8-32-29 ; 8-82-24 ; 3-45-1; 8-1-25; 2-16-3; 8-34-9).

In the prayer-mantras asking him to come to the Soma-drinking, carried by the horses that bear his chariot, Indra's immense numbers of horses are specified. He is prayed to come with horses numbering two, four, six, eight, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety and a hundred.

(2-18-4 to 7, 8-1-9).

In still other places this number exceeds even a thousand. For example, "Indra and Vāyu are both carried by horses numbering a thousand"

(4-46-3, 6-47-18 ; 8-1-24).

Because these horses of Indra have a supernatural form, exact knowledge of their form cannot be reached by the human eye. Therefore the question also arises naturally, "Who has the ability to see the two horses of Indra, who of you has seen them?" *[The opening quotation mark of this sentence is not closed in the supplied text; as supplied.]*

हरी इंद्रस्य नि चिकाय कः स्वित्. (*harī iṃdrasya ni cikāya kaḥ svit.*)

(10-114-9).

### Printed p. 641

*[The running head was merged with the text of page 640 in the supplied text; it was separated in kn.md. The word for Ṛgveda-saṃhitā in the head is printed with a different first letter; as supplied. The page-end of p. 640 also carries a stray line with the number 81, kept as supplied.]*

It is well known that Indra's chariot and horses were made by the Ṛbhus, the skilled craftsmen.

(1-111-1 ; 5-31-4).

Some passages, giving the purport seen below, tell of special qualities of Indra's chariot and horses. For example, the horses that bear Indra's chariot are described as having the eyes called sūracakṣus. (सूरचक्षसः (*sūracakṣasaḥ*)).

(1-6-2 ; 1-16-1, 2 , 1-55-7 ; 1-84-6 , 1-101-10 ; 2-11-6 ; 8-13-11, 27 ; 10-44-2)

Indra is praised as being carried at times by the horses of Sūrya, and at other times by the horses of Vāyu.

(10-49-7 ; 10-22-4 to 6)

The description of Indra sitting and travelling together with Vāyu in Vāyu's chariot, at times as charioteer and at other times as his friend, both in one chariot, shows greatly the relation between Indra and Vāyu and the speed of Indra's chariot.

(4-46-2 ; 4-48-2 ; 7-90-7)

Indra's horses, by the power of praise, themselves come to the chariot and are yoked. (ब्रह्मणा ते ब्रह्मयुजा युनज्मि हरी (*brahmaṇā te brahmayujā yunajmi harī*))

*[The closing bracket is printed without an opening one; as supplied.]*

(5-35-4 ; 1-82-6 ; 2-18-3 ; 8-1-24 ; 8-17-2 ; 8-2-27 ; 8-45-39 ; 8-86-9)

The purport is that, as soon as the prayer in the form of praise by the sacrificers is recited, Indra at once yokes the horses to the chariot in order to come to their sacrifice. Since praises are the cause for yoking the horses to the chariot, the idea is that the yoking of the horses takes place by the power of praise.

In this way, of the many Saṃhitā passages that describe the glorious chariot and horses of Indra, who travels over earth and the intermediate space, only a few have been explained above as examples.

**Indra's thunderbolt and other implements.**

Indra's great thunderbolt is well known to have been made by Tvaṣṭṛ, the divine craftsman. It is also stated that Tvaṣṭṛ made it for Indra himself. (त्वष्टास्मै वज्रं स्वर्यं ततक्ष (*tvaṣṭāsmai vajraṃ svaryaṃ tatakṣa*))-

(1-32-2 ; 1-61-6 ; 1-85-9 ; 5-31-4 ; 6-17-10 ; 10-48-3)

But in some places only, it is stated precisely that it was made by Kāvya-Uśanas and given to Indra for the killing of Asuras. (यं ते काव्य उशना . . . ततक्ष वज्रं (*yaṃ te kāvya uśanā . . . tatakṣa vajraṃ*)).

(1-121-12 ; 5-34-2)

### Printed p. 642

The creation of the thunderbolt and Indra's taking it up: on this matter a passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa speaks as follows.

देवा वै प्रथमेनाह्नेंद्राय वज्रं समभरंस्तं द्वितीयेनाह्नासिंचंस्तं तृतीयेनाह्ना प्रायच्छंस्तं चतुर्थेऽहन्ब्राहरत् ॥ (*devā vai prathamenāhneṃdrāya vajraṃ samabharaṃstaṃ dvitīyenāhnāsiṃcaṃstaṃ tṛtīyenāhnā prāyacchaṃstaṃ caturthe 'hanbrāharat ‖*)

(Ai. Brā. 4-1)

*[The reference is printed with the abbreviation ಇ. ಬ್ರಾ. at its head; as supplied.]*

The gods, for the proceedings of the first day, provided Indra with the thunderbolt; on the second day they consecrated (anointed) it; on the third day they handed it over to him; on the fourth day Indra wielded that thunderbolt given by the gods. So it is stated. And further: "The thunderbolt lies in the sea situated in the intermediate space, covered over by water."

(8-100-9)

In this account the natural order of the origin of the thunderbolt is described. In some places this thunderbolt is said to be of golden form (1-57-2, 1-85-9 ; 8-57-3 ; 10-23-3), and in some places to be golden-coloured together with emerald (10-96-3). In still other places it is said to be आयसः (*āyasaḥ*), that is, made of steel.

(1-52-8 ; 1-80-12 ; 1-81-4 ; 1-121-9 ; 8-85-3 ; 10-48-3 ; 10-96-3 ; 10-113-5).

यदेकः (*yadekaḥ*) . - . .” and so on — thus it is praised. It is stated that all the gods fear Indra precisely because he has this valour.

(5-30-5)

In 8-7-1 it is asked whether it was not an offence on the part of the Maruts that they did not help their friend Indra in a time of difficulty, and how, in such a situation, they can be worthy of trust.

In 4-18-11 Aditi, the mother of Indra, grieved that all the other gods had abandoned her son without helping him, approaches Viṣṇu and prays that he should help her son. But elsewhere there is also a somewhat different account of this. It is stated that while Indra was fighting the Asura Vṛtra, all the other gods, afraid of Vṛtra's terrible form, left Indra alone and ran away, and that Indra, because of his friendship with the Maruts, destroyed Vṛtra with their help.

(8-96-7)

Sāyaṇa has stated the purport in this context in such a way that there is no contradiction between the earlier statements and this one, and he has supported his meaning by citing a sentence of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa. The sentence of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa is as follows.—

इंद्रो वै वृत्तं हनिष्यन्सर्वा देवता अब्रवीदनु मोपतिष्ठध्वमुप मा ह्वयध्वमिति तथेति तं हनिष्यंत आद्रवन्नोऽवेन्मां वै हनिष्यंत आद्रवंति हंतेमान्फीषया इति तानभिप्राश्वसीत्तस्य श्वसथादीषमाणा विश्वे देवा अद्रवन् मरुतो हैनं नाजहुः प्रहर भगवो जहि वीरयस्वेत्येवैनमेतां वाचं वदंत उपातिष्ठंत । तदेतदृषिः पश्यन्नभ्यनूवाच वृत्रस्य त्वा श्वसथादीषमाणा विश्वे देवा अजहुर्ये सखायः। मरुद्भरिंद्र सख्यं ते अस्त्वथेमा विश्वाः पृतना जयासीति । सोऽवेदिमे वै किल मे सचिवा इमे माकामायंत हंतेमानस्मिन्नुक्थ आभजा इति ॥ (*iṃdro vai vṛttaṃ haniṣyansarvā devatā abravīdanu mopatiṣṭhadhvamupa mā hvayadhvamiti tatheti taṃ haniṣyaṃta ādravanno 'venmāṃ vai haniṣyaṃta ādravaṃti haṃtemānphīṣayā iti tānabhiprāśvasīttasya śvasathādīṣamāṇā viśve devā adravan maruto hainaṃ nājahuḥ prahara bhagavo jahi vīrayasvetyevainametāṃ vācaṃ vadaṃta upātiṣṭhaṃta | tadetadṛṣiḥ paśyannabhyanūvāca vṛtrasya tvā śvasathādīṣamāṇā viśve devā ajahurye sakhāyaḥ| marudbhariṃdra sakhyaṃ te astvathemā viśvāḥ pṛtanā jayāsīti | so 'vedime vai kila me sacivā ime mākāmāyaṃta haṃtemānasminnuktha ābhajā iti ‖*)

(Ai. Brā. 3-20)

Indra, wishing to kill the Asura Vṛtra, addressed all the gods: "O gods, follow me closely without leaving me, and be my helpers." Then they gave the assurance, "We shall do so", and pressed forward to kill Vṛtra. Then Vṛtra said, "These gods are pressing forward to kill me. I shall frighten them," and, letting out a powerful breath ನಿಟ್ಟಸುರನ್ನು, he made a terrible sound. Then all the gods who heard that terrible sound became terrified and ran in all directions. But the Maruts alone did not abandon Indra. Standing right beside Indra, they kept encouraging him: "O Indra, strike him. Show your valour." Then, praising the friendship of the Maruts, the sage recited the mantra beginning वृत्रस्य त्वा (*vṛtrasya tvā*) and praised them.

(8-96-7)

Then Indra said, "These Maruts alone are my true friends. They love me; therefore in the uktha offered to me I shall give them also a share."

In the Ṛk-saṃhitā, in the mantra 10-32-14, describing this same situation, it is praised with the words अहेर्यातारं (*aheryātāraṃ*). Here too the meaning is doubtful. It is stated here that at the time of the Asura Vṛtra even Indra felt some fear. Two or three kinds of purport can be given, for example that out of that fear he ran like a hawk, crossed the ninety-nine river streams that came in his way, and escaped. But that discussion is unnecessary at present. The help given to Indra by other gods too is praised in some places. For example—

"O Indra, as parents protect their children, the two Aśvin gods protected Indra in a time of distress. When, at the time of the manifestation of your valour, Soma was drunk, the goddess Sarasvatī stood by your side as a helper, with all her means of protection ರಕ್ಷಹಾಸಾಧನಗಳೊಂದಿಗೂ."

As soon as Indra manifests his valour and resolves, all the clouds stationed in the atmosphere scatter and the darkness is destroyed. The sun too, regaining his natural state, spreads everywhere the radiance that gives light to the whole world.

Regarding the matter described in Mantra 1-51-4, Sāyaṇa states his view as follows. Its original is this:

वृत्रं यदिंद्र शवसावधीरहिमादित्सूर्यं दिव्यारोहयो दृशे । (*vṛtraṃ yadiṃdra śavasāvadhīrahimāditsūryaṃ divyārohayo dṛśe |*)

Explaining the purport of this, Sāyaṇa says:

वृत्रेणावृतं सूर्यं तस्माद्वृतात् अमूमुच इत्यर्थः ॥ (*vṛtreṇāvṛtaṃ sūryaṃ tasmādvṛtāt amūmuca ityarthaḥ ‖*)

He has stated that the purport is that Indra freed the sun, covered by Vṛtra, from Vṛtra. But if the sentence of the original is examined, it indicates a meaning that, after the slaying of Vṛtra, he established the sun in the atmosphere. In short, the purport of this is that Indra became the cause of the destruction of darkness.

The situation of fighting thus with Vṛtra, who is of the form of darkness, is described in many places in the Ṛk-saṃhitā. The aim of the fight is to destroy the darkness and spread light.

(1-4-8 ; 1-32-1 ; 1-52-2 ; 1-54-4 ; 1-80-1 ; 1-103-2 ; 2-11-5 ; 5-32-1; 1-89-7 ; 10-113-6).

Of the Asuras who are enemies of Indra, one named Uraṇa is described as having ninety-nine arms and as a monster; his deformed form is described.

(2-14-4).

Another is stated to have had three heads and six eyes.

(10-99-6).

Such forms and imaginative descriptions are also fitting to natural circumstances. It is natural that people scorched by the heat of the burning summer sun look for rain as soon as the summer is over. But there are also many situations in which dense clouds pervade the whole atmosphere and yet do not pour rain; in such circumstances it is natural that the belief arises that some Asuric power is obstructing the rain. It is also natural that a kind of faith arises in the divine power that destroys this Asuric power. The appearance of thunder and lightning is described as the clash, in the atmosphere, of two powers, the divine and the Asuric.

Indra is the presiding deity who reflects this divine power. This power of Indra, helpful to the devotees and destroyer of their enemies, provides wealth to the sacrificer and others and averts from them the affliction caused by the Asuras. The masses of clouds moving in the atmosphere are described as chariots, as chariot-horses and as Indra's bearers.

It is understood that this Indra is a deity of a nature different from Parjanya. Since there are also passages in which Indra and Parjanya are compared, there is full scope to say that they are separate deities, each of his own nature. Many hymns addressed to Parjanya too show that he is a deity distinct from Indra.

(8-6-1).

But there are many passages that state the identity of Indra and the sun.

(8-9-30).

In many places the efforts the sacrificers make to bring Indra to their sacrifice are compared to the efforts of a fowler to catch birds. Moreover, there is competition among the sacrificers themselves in this matter. Fearing that others may stop Indra's horses, detain Indra somewhere and so spoil the chance of his coming to them, the sacrificers who are ready to offer Soma hurry ahead of all the rest, stop Indra as a bird is stopped by a net, and pray that he come to their sacrifice. The sense of some passages that carry this idea may be examined here as examples.

"I shall stop Indra's horses even before others can do so. O Indra, be pleased with my words of praise and come to me. Do not stay there, drawn by the praises of other sacrificers, for they call you just as I do."

Even when the rites of the former sacrificer are excellent, he sometimes prefers the rites of another sacrificer that are defective. No one can obstruct his independence. But the occasions when he is close to those who worship him are the more numerous.

(6-47-17).

In the passage quoted above, that is, in stating the sense of mantra 6-47-16, one situation gives some room for discussion. In mantra 16 the word एधमानद्विट् (*edhamānadviṭ*) is an epithet of Indra and tells his nature. The word एधमान (*edhamāna*) means one who is growing, that is, one possessed of wealth and so on and of mental comfort. But the question arises naturally whether Indra is one who fosters enmity with those who have wealth, and whether there is then no distinction between friend and foe. Therefore Sāyaṇa, in this context, explains it as the enemy of the selfish who, having grown in wealth, do not offer oblations in sacrifices and other rites: असुन्वतां विधमानानां (*asunvatāṃ vidhamānānāṃ*). The word विधमानद्विट् (*vidhamānadviṭ*) applies in general to all the gods. It becomes clear from this that the gods cannot bear the prosperity of men. The sense of the next mantra supports the same view. The scholar Wilson says as follows.

*[Printed oddities: in the sentence that runs over the page break the supplied text reads ಇಂದ್ರಮ, rendered here as "Indra"; the one word विधमानद्विट् (*vidhamānadviṭ*) is also printed as विधमानिद्विट् (*vidhamānidviṭ*) below and the explanation is cited as विधमानानां (*vidhamānānāṃ*); all as supplied.]*

"He is also represented in the same hymn as of a capricious temperament, neglecting those who serve him, and favouring those who pay him no adoration ; a notion somewhat at variance with a doctrine, previously inculcated that the ceremonial worship of Indra is able to atone for the most atrocious crimes".

(quoted by Muir. Original Sanskrit Texts. Vol. V. p. 111).

The sense of these words is as follows. One may say that the meaning given by the English commentators for विधमानिद्विट् (*vidhamānidviṭ*) is natural. For immediately after this mantra, the statement in the next mantra, "Indra behaves as he pleases; Indra is ready to leave the sacrificer who offers oblations and go to one who does not offer them", supports the sense above. There is a complete contradiction between what is described in the mantras (5-34-4), whose sense is that sins of every kind are destroyed if an oblation is offered to Indra in a sacrifice, and what is said in the present mantras. This is Wilson's opinion. For this contradiction to disappear, as Sāyaṇa and the author of the Nirukta say, it has to be taken as: विधमानानां वर्धमानानां असुन्वतां द्विट् (*vidhamānānāṃ vardhamānānāṃ asunvatāṃ dviṭ*), the enemy of all who are growing without offering oblations. That fits the situation.

**Some apparent inconsistencies that may appear to the superficial view in the description of Indra's nature, and the answer to them.**

To those who have no acquaintance with the Ṛk-saṃhitā, whether through study of the original or through a translation, it is natural that some contradictory points should appear in the description of Indra's nature given above. But that is itself natural. If one examines the matter only from the superficial point of view, there is no doubt that the descriptions above show inconsistencies. The description that Indra is the supreme deity who governs and supports the universe is contrary to the other, ordinary descriptions of his qualities. For example: in the drinking of Soma and in other dealings, wishes and the like such as ordinary human beings have are described in Indra. At times even desire for the objects of the senses seems to be intense.

Such a description of his nature does not agree with the extraordinary, supernatural, guiding-for-the-whole-world and spiritual great qualities of Indra. There are also occasions on which passages describing such contrary natures occur in one and the same sūkta. But if the matter is examined here from the spiritual point of view, it is understood that such a nature is quite natural. How?

In all the elements of the universe two kinds of nature can be seen: one eternal, the other non-eternal; one belonging to the senses, the other spiritual; one ordinary, the other extraordinary. In this way this variety is plainly present in every human being. It is natural that this variety should be found also in a deity who pervades the universe. Because he pervades the universe, the ordinary qualities natural to the universe, and because he transcends the universe, extraordinary, supernatural, divine qualities, are found together in him; there is no inconsistency in this.

Even if one supposes that the qualities such as desire show a worldly nature in Indra, it is established that it is not a description of desire for the objects of the senses in the sense of modern culture. The intense desire that Indra shows in the drinking of Soma and the like is not reckoned as desire for objects of the senses. The Soma that obtains immortality for all its worshippers, the desire for such Soma juice, which brings about immortality, is certainly a supernatural and divine desire, and it is certain that it is not a fault. Since these contrary qualities are described by one and the same ṛṣi, it is not right to say that such words of a ṛṣi are inconsistent. A few such occasions may be examined. For example:

*[The word printed ಸ್ಕೂಲವಾದ (and again in a compound a few lines below) is rendered here as "superficial", as supplied. The word ಅದ ಇಂದ್ರನ in the sentence on the extraordinary qualities is printed so; as supplied.]*

"Indra established the heaven in the empty region. He stood pervading heaven and earth entirely. He supported the earth and made it spread out wide. All these extraordinary deeds Indra did by the power of drinking Soma juice."

(2-15-2).

Even when examined from the spiritual point of view there is no doubt that these descriptions are indeed descriptions of Indra's divine qualities.

**Some passages describing the mutual relation of Indra and Varuṇa.**

In the early Maṇḍalas of the Ṛk-saṃhitā the sūktas addressed to Indra are in the majority; in the last Maṇḍalas the sūktas addressed to Varuṇa are in greater number. For this reason some English scholars have held the opinion that in the early period of the composition of the Ṛk-saṃhitā greater importance was given to Indra than to Varuṇa, and that in the last period greater reverence was shown to Varuṇa than to Indra. There are no proper grounds for this opinion. And it can be said that it is a wrong opinion.

I have explained before, and shall explain further, what the Saṃhitā passages themselves tell: that all the worldly differences such as Indra and Varuṇa are different special manifestations of one and the same principle, and that these names are not kinds of deities with a difference of principle. इंद्रं मित्रं वरुणमाहु: (*iṃdraṃ mitraṃ varuṇamāhu:*)) Nevertheless, to support the point that even in the description of the special manifestations of the one principle there is no room for such a difference, some passages that describe these two deities, whether together or individually, may be examined.

*[The closing bracket after the Sanskrit words above has no opening bracket in the supplied text; as supplied. The Sanskrit words end in a colon in the supplied text, not in a visarga; as supplied.]*

इंद्रावरुणयोरहं सम्राजोरव आ वृणे । शा नो मृळात ईदृते ॥ (*iṃdrāvaruṇayorahaṃ samrājorava ā vṛṇe | śā no mṛḷāta īdṛte ‖*)

The point described in the mantras that use the word अनिंद्र (*aniṃdra*) is noteworthy. This word is used on many occasions.

(1-133-1 ; 4-23-7 ; 5-2-3 ; 7-18-16 ; 10-23-6 ; 10-48-7).

अनिंद्र (*aniṃdra*) means one who is not a worshipper of Indra. By this word either non-Āryas who do not worship Indra and the other gods, or the demonic powers hostile to Indra, may be understood.

In the twelfth sūkta of the second Maṇḍala the description of the great qualities of Indra is of the highest order. Only some of them may be examined here. They describe Indra's power of governing the universe.

The exceedingly wise Indra, as soon as he was born, surpassed all the other gods by his great power. O men, know him to be Indra, at whose strength and might heaven and earth trembled.

*[The word printed ಮಾರಿದ್ದನು in the sentence above is printed so in the supplied text; it is rendered "surpassed", as supplied. The dash printed after it is kept in the Kannada; the quotation has no opening mark in the supplied text.]*

(2-12).

O men, he who made the trembling earth stand firm, who made the agitated mountains immovable, who created the vast atmosphere and who upheld the heavenly world, know him to be Indra.

(2-12-2).

"I, who am the soul of the gods, have obtained, only with the help of the Ādityas and the other gods, very powerful strength, an unconquerable state and unobstructed manly vigour. Therefore I shall not bring ruin upon the excellent states of the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Maruts, the sons of Rudra."

### Printed p. 683

*[The sentence above begins at the foot of p. 682 and ends at the head of p. 683, in the middle of a word (pages 682 and 683); the two parts are joined here. The supplied text has the closing quotation mark but no opening one; as supplied.]*

These words of Indra (10-48-11) show the circumstance in which Indra expresses his gratitude towards the other gods.

Having explained the sense of some of the praising passages which say that Indra alone performed extraordinary deeds that the other gods could not perform, we bring this section to a close.

Indra alone, who surpasses men and does not need the help of others, possesses strength greater than that of all living beings. And he also possesses strength that cannot be conquered by anyone.

*[The word printed ಮಾರಿದವನೂ in the sentence above, from the same root as the word noted on the previous page, is rendered "surpasses", as supplied.]*

(8-62-2).

All the remaining gods also, praising the excellent manly vigour and valour of Indra, make their humility known.

(8-63-7).

May our praise addressed to Indra be true, and may there be no kind of falsity in it. The most severe calamity befalls one who does not offer Soma juice to Indra. But the devotee who worships Indra by offering Soma obtains abundant wealth accompanied by great light.

(8-62-12).

There is no god equal to Indra. Therefore there is no possibility at all that any god with qualities surpassing his exists.

(4-30-1).

This Indra alone conquered all the gods in battle. And even the most ancient gods, knowing the power of Indra, showed their humility before him and acknowledged his lordship.

(7-21-7).

Varuṇa, Sūra and all the other gods also bow to the rule laid down by Indra and carry out their duties.

(1-101-3).

Indra alone conquered all the enemies who were equal to the gods Mitra, Aryaman and Varuṇa (10-89-2, 9). From such passages it is understood that Indra is the one who has the greatest power of all the gods named in them.

The Pīṭhikā (introduction) is concluded.

**The thirtieth sūkta** (ಮೂವತ್ತನೆಯ ಸೂಕ್ತವು)

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> तृतीयेनुवाके नव सूक्तानि । तत्रेच्छंति त्वेति द्वाविंशत्यृचं प्रथमं

> आ. ३-८ । इति सूत्रितं ॥ स्वस्तये वाजिभिश्चेत्येषैंद्रे पशौ हविषो याज्या । सूत्रितं

> शुनं हुवेम मघवानमिंद्रमश्वायंतो गव्यंतो वाजयंतः । आ. २-२० । इति ॥

**Anuvāda (Kannada).** In the third anuvāka of the third Maṇḍala there are nine sūktas. Among them the sūkta beginning इच्छंति त्वा (*icchaṃti tvā*) is the first. There are twenty-two Ṛks in it. In the Anukramaṇikā it is said: इच्छंति द्व्यधिकैंद्रं (*icchaṃti dvyadhikaiṃdraṃ*). The seer of this sūkta is Viśvāmitra, the seer of the Maṇḍala; the deity is Indra; the metre is Triṣṭubh. In the Abhiplana *[so printed, differently from the bhāṣya block; as supplied]* sacrifice and in the sacrifice called Daśarātra, on the first day, at the midday pressing, among the śastra mantras recited by the ṛtvij called Acchāpāka , this sūkta is to be recited in the place of the Ahīna-sūkta as the second Sampāta-sūkta; this is explained in the section called अभिप्लवपृष्ट्याहानि (*abhiplavapṛṣṭyāhāni*) of the Āśvalāyana-śrauta-sūtra by the sūtra इमामूष्टिच्छंति त्वा शासद्वह्निरिति संपाताः (*imāmūṣṭicchaṃti tvā śāsadvahniriti saṃpātāḥ*) *[the first word is printed so, differently from the bhāṣya block; as supplied]* (Ā. 7-5).

In the animal sacrifice offered to Indra under the name Vṛtraghna, the Ṛk सहदानुं (*sahadānuṃ*) (the 8th Ṛk of this sūkta) is to be recited as the yājyā mantra in the vapā offering; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana-śrauta-sūtra सहदानुं पुरुहूत क्षियंतं स्तुत इंद्रो मघवा यद्ध वृत्रा (*sahadānuṃ puruhūta kṣiyaṃtaṃ stuta iṃdro maghavā yaddha vṛtrā*) *[the last word is printed with a long final vowel, differently from the bhāṣya block; as supplied]* (Ā. 3-8). In the animal sacrifice offered to Indra, the application is explained by the sūtra स्वस्तये वाजिभिश्च प्रणेतः शुची वो हव्या मरुतः शुचीनां (*svastaye vājibhiśca praṇetaḥ śucī vo havyā marutaḥ śucīnāṃ*) *[the sixth word is printed so, differently from the bhāṣya block; as supplied]* (Ā. 3-7) *[the Anuvāda does not name the Ṛk to which this application belongs; as supplied]*.

In the Śunāsīra sacrifice, in the homa offered to the deity named Indra-Śuna, the Ṛk शुनं हुवेम (*śunaṃ huvema*) (the 22nd Ṛk of this sūkta) is to be recited as the anuvākyā mantra; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana-śrauta-sūtra शुनं हुवेम मघवानमिंद्रमश्वायंतो गव्यंतो वाजयंतः (*śunaṃ huvema maghavānamiṃdramaśvāyaṃto gavyaṃto vājayaṃtaḥ*) (Ā. 2-20).

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Viśvāmitra praises Indra: the priests worthy of Soma, his friends, press Soma and hold oblations for him, endure the harm done by rivals; no one else is so renowned. The rest of the bhāṣya is grammatical notes on सोम्यासः (*somyāsaḥ*), सुन्वंति (*sunvaṃti*), दधति (*dadhati*), तितिक्षंते (*titikṣaṃte*), अभिशस्तिं (*abhiśastiṃ*) and प्रकेतः (*praketaḥ*), mostly on accent.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- सोम्यासः (*somyāsaḥ*)—the ṛtvijs who possess Soma juice
- त्वा (*tvā*)—you
- इच्छंति (*icchaṃti*)—they desire
- सखायः (*sakhāyaḥ*)—the ṛtvijs who are your friends
- सोमं (*somaṃ*)—the Soma juice
- सुन्वंति (*sunvaṃti*)—they press and prepare
- प्रयांसि (*prayāṃsi*)—the food in the form of oblation
- दधति (*dadhati*)—they hold (in the confidence of your help)
- जनानां (*janānāṃ*)—given by the enemy people
- अभिशस्तिं (*abhiśastiṃ*)—the harm also
- तितिक्षंते (*titikṣaṃte*)—they endure
- त्वत् (*tvat*)—than you; कश्चन हि (*kaścana hi*)—who else indeed; आ प्रकेतः (*ā praketaḥ*)—is of complete renown?

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, the ṛtvijs who possess Soma juice desire you. The ṛtvijs who are your friends press and prepare the Soma juice *[the Kannada word for "Soma juice" is printed here without its middle syllable; as supplied]* and also hold food in the form of oblation. Trusting in your help, they endure even the harm caused by their enemies. Who else is more renowned than you?

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
The bearers of the libations desire you; your friends pour forth the Soma juice ; they offer copious oblations : (supported by you) they endure patiently the calumny of men, for who is so renowed [sic] as you are ?

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

No place is too far for Indra; he should come quickly with his horses, for the pressings are done and the stones are ready as the fire blazes. The rest is grammar and accent notes on याहि (*yāhi*), हरिवः (*harivaḥ*), स्थिराय (*sthirāya*), सवना (*savanā*) and समिधाने (*samidhāne*).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- हरिवः (*harivaḥ*)—O Indra, who are endowed with horses of tawny colour; परमा चित् रजांसि (*paramā cit rajāṃsi*)—even the most distant worlds
- ते (*te*)—for you; दूरे न (*dūre na*)—are not distant (therefore, however far away you may be *[the parenthesis is not closed in the print; as supplied]*
- हरिभ्यां (*haribhyāṃ*)—together with your horses
- तु (*tu*)—quickly; आ प्र याहि (*ā pra yāhi*)—come towards our sacrifice
- स्थिराय (*sthirāya*)—to you who are firm in resolve
- वृष्णे (*vṛṣṇe*)—and a showerer of desires; इमा सवना (*imā savanā*)—these rites, the morning pressing and the others
- कृता (*kṛtā*)—are performed
- अग्नौ (*agnau*)—when Agni
- समिधाने (*samidhāne*)—is just kindled
- ग्रावाणः (*grāvāṇaḥ*)—the stones that press out the juice
- युक्ताः (*yuktāḥ*)—are ready to press the Soma *[the print has a different last letter here, ಸೋನು, than the ಸೋಮ of the Bhāvārtha; as supplied]*

*[In the print the words meaning "for you" are broken across two lines, ನಿನ and ಗಾಗಿ, without a hyphen; as supplied.]*

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, who are endowed with horses of tawny colour, even the most distant worlds do not seem distant to you. Therefore, however far away you may be, come quickly together with your horses towards our sacrifice. These rites, the morning pressing and the others, are performed for you, who are firm in resolve and a showerer of desires. As soon as the Āhavanīya fire is kindled, the stones are ready to press the Soma juice. *[The print has a stray word, ರಹ, after "however far away you may be"; as supplied. The last sentence has no closing clause of its own in the Kannada; translated as printed.]*

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Master of tawny steeds, the remotest regions are not remote for you then come quickly with your horses: to you, the steady showerer (of benefits), these sacrifices are presented ; the stones (for bruising the Soma) are ready as the fire is being kindled.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Addressing Indra, the showerer: where now are the heroic deeds you once performed against the Asuras when you were pressed in battle? The rest is grammar and accent notes on सुशिप्रः (*suśipraḥ*), तरुत्रः (*tarutraḥ*), महाव्रातः (*mahāvrātaḥ*), तुविकूर्मिः (*tuvikūrmiḥ*), ऋघावान् (*ṛghāvān*) and क्व (*kva*).

*[The label Pratipadārtha is printed twice in succession, the first time with nothing after it; kept as supplied.]*

- वृषभ (*vṛṣabha*)—O Indra, showerer of desires
- इंद्रः (*iṃdraḥ*)—possessed of all lordship
- सुशिप्रः (*suśipraḥ*)—having an excellent helmet
- मघवा (*maghavā*)—wealthy
- तरुत्रः (*tarutraḥ*)—who carries across out of calamity
- महाव्रातः (*mahāvrātaḥ*)—united with the great host (of the Maruts)
- तुविकूर्मिः (*tuvikūrmiḥ*)—who carries out many (in battle)

*(Ṛk 3, Pratipadārtha, continued; the entry for तुविकूर्मिः (*tuvikūrmiḥ*) breaks across pages 688 and 689.)*

heroic deeds *[the print has ವೀತ್ಯಕರ್ಮ here and in the next entries, but ವೀರ್ಯಕರ್ಮ in the Bhāvārtha; as supplied]*; ऋघावान् (*ṛghāvān*)—destroyer of enemies; उग्र (*ugra*)—you who are terrible to the enemy; बाधितः (*bādhitaḥ*)—when resisted by the enemies; मर्त्येषु (*martyeṣu*)—in regard to those deadly Asuras; यत् (*yat*)—which heroic deeds; धाः (*dhāḥ*)—you manifested; ते (*te*)—your; त्या वीर्याणि (*tyā vīryāṇi*)—those heroic deeds; क्व (*kva*)—where now?

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, showerer of desires, you who are possessed of all lordship, have an excellent helmet, are wealthy, carry across out of calamity, are united with the great host of the Maruts, carry out many heroic deeds in battle, destroy enemies and are terrible to the enemy: when you were resisted by the enemies, where now are those heroic deeds which you manifested in regard to those deadly Asuras?

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
*(The printed label is "English Translations".)* Showerer (of benefits, you are) Indra, the wearer of the helmet, the professor [sic] of opulence, the conveyer (of men beyond evil), the leader of the numerous troop (of the Maruts), the achiever of many great deeds, the devastator of hostile (regions), the terror of your foes; where are those heroic deeds (which you have performed) against the mortal (Asuras) when opposed (by them in battle)?

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Indra, alone and unaided, goes about casting the firmly placed Asuras down from their places and destroying the sinful; heaven, earth and mountains stand firm in obedience to his command. The rest is grammar and accent notes on स्म (*sma*), च्यावयन् (*cyāvayan*), चरसि (*carasi*), जिघ्नमानः (*jighnamānaḥ*), द्यावापृथिवी (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), निमितेव (*nimiteva*) and तस्थुः (*tasthuḥ*).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- त्वं (*tvaṃ*)—you
- एकः (*ekaḥ*)—alone, without anyone's help
- अच्युतानि (*acyutāni*)—the firmly established Asuras
- च्यावयन् (*cyāvayan*)—casting them down from their places
- वृत्रा (*vṛtrā*)—the sinful ones
- जिघ्नमानः (*jighnamānaḥ*)—harming; चरसि हि स्म (*carasi hi sma*)—you go about, do you not?
- तव (*tava*)—your
- व्रताय (*vratāya*)—obeying the command
- द्यावापृथिवी (*dyāvāpṛthivī*)—heaven and earth
- पर्वतासः (*parvatāsaḥ*)—the mountains
- निमितेव (*nimiteva*)—having an immovable base; अनु तस्थुः (*anu tasthuḥ*)—stand firm

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, you alone, without anyone's help, go about casting the firmly established Asuras down from their places and harming the sinful, do you not? Obeying your command, heaven and earth and the mountains stand firm and immovable.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
*(The printed label is "English Translation.")* You alone casting down the firmly-footed (Asuras) proceed, destroying the Vritras, and obedient to your command the heaven and earth and the mountains stood as if immoveable.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Indra, invoked by many and endowed with prowess, as slayer of Vritra told the gods not to fear the Asuras, and this word is true; his might, by which he holds heaven and earth together, is famous. The rest is grammar and accent notes on अभये (*abhaye*), अवदः (*avadaḥ*), अपारे (*apāre*), संगृह्नासि (*saṃgṛhnāsi*) and काशिः (*kāśiḥ*); the block ends with printed double bars and the figure 1, as supplied.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- पुरुहूत (*puruhūta*)—O you who are called by many; उत इंद्र (*uta iṃdra*)—O Indra
- श्रवोभिः (*śravobhiḥ*)—endowed with heroic deeds
- एकः (*ekaḥ*)—and helpless (unaided), you; वृत्रहा सन् (*vṛtrahā san*)—as the destroyer of the Asura Vṛtra
- आभये (*ābhaye*)—which word of reassurance, that there is no need to fear the Asuras *[the print has a stray quotation mark before this entry's meaning; as supplied]*
- आवदः (*āvadaḥ*)—you spoke
- दृढं (*dṛḍhaṃ*)—that is true
- मघवन् (*maghavan*)—O Indra; अपारे चित् (*apāre cit*)—although extremely distant; इमे रोदसी (*ime rodasī*)—these heaven and earth
- यत् (*yat*)—by which of your greatness
- संगृछ्णाः (*saṃgṛchṇāḥ*)—you hold together
- ते (*te*)—such greatness of yours
- काशिरित् (*kāśirit*)—is indeed well known in the world

*[The Pratipadārtha entry संगृछ्णाः (*saṃgṛchṇāḥ*) differs in spelling from the Saṃhitā and bhāṣya forms; as supplied.]*

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, called by many for help, you who are endowed with heroic deeds *[the print has ವೀಶ್ಯಗಳಿಂದ here, evidently for "heroic deeds"; as supplied]* and are unaided, as the destroyer of the Asura Vṛtra you told the gods not to fear, and that word proved true. O Indra, by which greatness of yours you hold together even the boundless heaven and earth, that greatness of yours is indeed well known in the world.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Indra, may your chariot drawn by two horses go swiftly against the enemies, your thunderbolt destroy them; slay those who face you, follow you or flee, and make the whole world true. The rest is grammar and accent notes on प्रवता (*pravatā*), प्रमृणन् (*pramṛṇan*), जहि (*jahi*), प्रतीचः (*pratīcaḥ*), पराचः (*parācaḥ*), कृणुहि (*kṛṇuhi*) and अस्तु (*astu*).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- ते (*te*)—your
- हरिभ्यां (*haribhyāṃ*)—the chariot yoked with horses
- प्रवता (*pravatā*)—(towards the enemies) in your region
- सु (*su*)—swiftly; प्र एतु (*pra etu*)—let it come exceedingly
- ते (*te*)—your
- वज्रः (*vajraḥ*)—thunderbolt
- शत्रून् (*śatrūn*)—the Asuras
- प्रम्यणन् (*pramyaṇan*)—harming *[the print has a letter differing from the Saṃhitā's प्रमृणन् (*pramṛṇan*); as supplied]*

*[The supplied text of this window ends in the middle of the Pratipadārtha of Ṛk 6, with the next entry begun by the lone syllable प्र (*pra*); the Pratipadārtha of Ṛk 6 continues in the next window.]*

### Printed p. 693

*(Ṛk 6, Pratipadārtha, continued from page 692: the entry begun there by the lone syllable ಪ್ರ goes on.)*

…quickly; let it be hurled upon them *[the print has ತೀಘ್ರವಾಗಿ, evidently for "quickly"; as supplied]*; प्रतीचः (*pratīcaḥ*)—the enemies who face you and resist you; जहि (*jahi*)—destroy; अनूचः (*anūcaḥ*)—also the enemies who chase you from behind; पराचः (*parācaḥ*)—also those who are frightened of you and run away (destroy them completely; when the enemies have been destroyed completely in this way) विश्वं (*viśvaṃ*)—the whole world also; सत्यं (*satyaṃ*)—as one intent on rites of a true nature; कृणुहि (*kṛṇuhi*)—make; विष्टं अस्तु (*viṣṭaṃ astu*)—(such capacity) let it be established in you.

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, let your chariot yoked with horses come swiftly towards the enemy. Let your thunderbolt be hurled swiftly upon the Asuras so as to destroy them. Destroy completely the enemies who face you and resist, those who chase you from behind and those who flee in fear of you. When the enemies have been slain in this way, make the whole world intent on rites of a true nature. May all such capacity be established in you.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Let (your car),Indra, drawn by your horses (rush) downwards (upon the Asuras); let your destroying thunderbolt fall upon your enemies; slay those that assail in front or in rear, or that fly (from the combat): make the universe (the abode of) truth ; (let such power) be concentrated in you.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Indra, to the man to whom you give vigour, wealth never gained before comes; your wisdom is auspicious and your gift of wealth boundless. A Ṛgveda mantra is cited; the rest is grammar and accent notes on धायुः (*dhāyuḥ*), अदधाः (*adadhāḥ*), मर्त्याय (*martyāya*), गेह्यं (*gehyaṃ*), सुमतिः (*sumatiḥ*) and रातिः (*rātiḥ*).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- धायुः (*dhāyuḥ*)—you who give unending wealth; यस्मै मर्त्याय (*yasmai martyāya*)—to whichever man
- अदधाः (*adadhāḥ*)—you give vigour
- सः (*saḥ*)—that man; अभक्तं चित् (*abhaktaṃ cit*)—such as was never seen before
- गेह्यं (*gehyaṃ*)—wealth fit for a house, in the form of gold, cattle and the like
- भजते (*bhajate*)—obtains
- पुरुहूत (*puruhūta*)—O Indra, who are called by many
- घृताची (*ghṛtācī*)—which is to be reached by the offering of oblations
- ते (*te*)—your
- सुमतिः (*sumatiḥ*)—excellent mind
- भद्रा (*bhadrā*)—is auspicious
- रातिः (*rātiḥ*)—(your) power of giving also
- सहस्रदाना (*sahasradānā*)—is a giver of immeasurable wealth

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, you who give unending wealth, the man in whom you create vigour obtains, in his own house, wealth never seen before, in the form of gold, cattle and the like. O Indra, called by many, your excellent mind, which is to be reached by the offering of oblations, brings about well-being. Your power of giving also bestows immeasurable wealth.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
The man to whom you grant, lord of power, (your good will), enjoys unprecedented domestic (prosperity): Indra, you are invoked by many,your auspicious favour, which is obtained by oblations, is the giver of unbounded wealth.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

सहस्रदाना (*sahasradānā*)—अपरिमितधनदानसमेता (*aparimitadhanadānasametā*). Here the word सहस्र (*sahasra*) has the meaning "many, immeasurable". The main sense is that Indra gives abundant wealth and the like to those who worship and praise him. The commentator has given, as examples, the Ṛks which explain this sense in detail—

### Printed p. 695

*(Ṛk 7, Special Topics, continued from page 694: the sentence breaks off before the Ṛks quoted at the top of this page.)*

दश ते कलशानां हिरण्यानामधीमहि । भूरिदा असि वृत्रहन् ॥ (*daśa te kalaśānāṃ hiraṇyānāmadhīmahi | bhūridā asi vṛtrahan ‖*) भूरिदा भूरि देहि नो मा दभ्रं भूर्या भर । भूरि फेदिंद्र दित्ससि ॥ (*bhūridā bhūri dehi no mā dabhraṃ bhūryā bhara | bhūri phediṃdra ditsasi ‖*) भूरिदा ह्यसि श्रुतः पुरुत्रा शूर वृत्रहन् ॥ आ नो भजस्व राधसि ॥ (*bhūridā hyasi śrutaḥ purutrā śūra vṛtrahan ‖ ā no bhajasva rādhasi ‖*) (Kha. Saṃ. 4-32-19, 20, 21) *[the abbreviation is printed with the first letter of "Kha"; as supplied]* — the commentator has given these Ṛks as examples. This idea is indicated in many other Ṛks as well.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Indra crushed the handless Kuṇāru, accompanied by Dānu, and slew the growing, footless Vṛtra by his might; alternatively Vṛtra is the cloud, as Yāska says. The grammar begins with सहदानुं (*sahadānuṃ*); the supplied text breaks off in the grammar on कुणारुं (*kuṇāruṃ*) at the syllables ಕುಣ. The bhāṣya has पुरूहूतेंद्र (*purūhūteṃdra*) where the Saṃhitā has पुरुहूत (*puruhūta*); as supplied.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- पुरुहूत (*puruhūta*)—O one called by many
- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- सहदानुं (*sahadānuṃ*)—who dwells with the Dānavī, the mother of Vṛtra
- क्षियंतं (*kṣiyaṃtaṃ*)—who is a doer of violence
- कुणारुं (*kuṇāruṃ*)—and who makes noise, such an asura
- अहस्तं (*ahastaṃ*)—having made him handless; सं पिणक् (*saṃ piṇak*)—destroy (him)
- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- वर्धमानं (*vardhamānaṃ*)—who grows
- पियारुं (*piyāruṃ*)—and who causes trouble
- वृत्रं (*vṛtraṃ*)—the asura Vṛtra
- अपादं (*apādaṃ*)—having made him footless
- तवसा (*tavasā*)—by your strength; अभि जघंथ (*abhi jaghaṃtha*)—destroy (him)

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, you who are called by many, make the asura who dwells with the Dānavī, the mother of Vṛtra, who is a doer of violence and makes noise, handless, and destroy him. O Indra, make the asura Vṛtra, who grows and causes trouble, footless, and destroy him by your strength.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Indra, you are invoked by many, grind to dust the reviling malevolent Vritra opposing you, dwelling with the mother of the Danavas, and increasing in might, until having deprived him of hand and foot, you have destroyed him by your strength.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

व्रत्रं वर्धमानं (*vratraṃ vardhamānaṃ*)—the growing Vṛtra. Or: वृणोत्याच्छादयति नभ इति वृत्रो मेघः ॥ तमिमं वर्धमानं मेघं (*vṛṇotyācchādayati nabha iti vṛtro meghaḥ ‖ tamimaṃ vardhamānaṃ meghaṃ*). Because it spreads over the sky and covers it, the word vṛtra has the sense of "cloud". The sense is also that Indra struck this growing, that is, swelling, cloud. In this matter the commentator has quoted स इषुमात्रमिषुमात्रं विष्ण्वज्जवर्धते (*sa iṣumātramiṣumātraṃ viṣṇvajjavardhate*) (Kṛ. Saṃ. 2-4-12-2), a sentence of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (of the Yajurveda). That is, the meaning explained here is that this Vṛtrāsura grew every day by the measure of one bow each time.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Indra, who makes the earth even and puts it in its place, and holds up heaven and the sky, is asked to let the waters sent by him flow down here. The bhāṣya reads एवापारामिषरां (*evāpārāmiṣarāṃ*) (joined by sandhi with the preceding words) at its beginning where the Pada-pāṭha has इषिरां (*iṣirāṃ*), and the supplied text has निषसत्प (*niṣasatpa*) where the Pada-pāṭha has ससत्थ (*sasattha*); as supplied.
